question: A feed has WKDY in calendar.txt (Mon to Fri) and a row WKDY, 20260704, exception_type 1 for Saturday July 4. What happens on July 4?
options: Nothing, Saturdays are 0 in calendar.txt so the exception is ignored
The feed is invalid because the date is outside the weekly pattern
Only trips with times past 24:00:00 run
All WKDY trips run on July 4 as an added service day
explain: exception_type 1 adds service on that date even though the weekly pattern says no. calendar_dates.txt modifies calendar.txt; that is exactly how special event or holiday services are added.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: A hot function has IPC 0.25 and 20 last-level cache misses per 1000 instructions. Which change is most likely to make it faster?
options: Rewrite it to execute 10% fewer instructions with the same memory access pattern
Change the data layout so consecutive iterations touch the same cache lines
Compile with a higher optimization level to shorten the instruction sequence
Run it on a core with a wider decoder
explain: Low IPC with many cache misses means the core is mostly waiting on memory. Removing instructions or widening the front end does little while every miss still stalls. Better locality cuts the misses that the cycles are actually spent on.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: TopdownL1 shows 60% backend bound, and drilling down shows most of it is memory bound. IPC is 0.4. Which next step fits best?
options: Reduce branch mispredictions with likely/unlikely hints
Shrink the binary so it fits in the instruction cache
Sample a cache-miss event with :pp to find the loads responsible, then improve their locality
Ignore it: backend bound means the CPU is doing useful work
explain: Memory bound means slots are lost waiting on data. Bad speculation and frontend fixes target other buckets. Precise sampling on a miss event points at the exact loads to restructure.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: With the defaults, what does setting khugepaged/max_ptes_none to 0 trade away?
options: Faults no longer allocate huge pages
khugepaged will not collapse any range with even one unpopulated PTE, so sparse regions stay on 4 KiB pages but never bloat
Huge pages can no longer be swapped
khugepaged stops running
explain: max_ptes_none only governs collapse: at 0, a range must have all 512 PTEs populated. That removes collapse-induced bloat but fewer ranges become huge. Fault-time allocation is controlled by enabled and defrag, not this knob.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Jamba-v0.1's config has 32 layers, attn_layer_period 8 and attn_layer_offset 4. Which layers (0-based) are attention?
explain: Attention sits where layer index mod 8 equals 4: layers 4, 12, 20 and 28. The other 28 layers are Mamba, giving the 1:7 ratio.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Convex combination: normalize, then weight with alpha
question: After min-max normalization, a query whose dense results all have cosine 0.80 to 0.81 gets dense scores spread from 0 to 1. What is the risk?
options: None; normalization makes scores comparable by design
Cosine scores become negative
Tiny, possibly meaningless cosine differences are stretched to the full range and can outweigh real BM25 differences
BM25 scores are rescaled to match the cosine range
explain: Min-max always maps the list's min to 0 and max to 1, regardless of how close they were. Our toy shows a milder version: a 0.11 cosine range became 0 to 1. Theoretical min-max (dividing from the known lower bound, -1 for cosine) keeps such near-ties close.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: You normalize the HyDE mean vector to length 1 before searching an inner-product index. What happens to the top-10 results?
options: They stay the same; only the score values change
They change, because longer vectors favor longer documents
They improve, because cosine is always better than inner product
They get worse, because the query contribution is removed
explain: Dividing the query vector by its positive length scales every document's score by the same factor, so the ordering is identical. Document vectors are untouched, so this is not the same as switching the whole index from inner product to cosine.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
question: You pick four matches for the DLT, but three of them lie on one straight line. What happens?
options: The DLT still works because 8 equations are enough
SVD returns the identity matrix
The fourth point is automatically ignored
The solution is degenerate: A loses rank and H is not determined
explain: Collinear points do not pin down the projective map; the system has a bigger null space and many H fit. OpenCV's findHomography docs say its robust methods discard collinear 4-point subsets for this reason.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
question: An epoll-based proxy wakes up and `epoll_wait` reports 50 readable sockets. How many system calls does it take to read all of them, and how many with io_uring if it submits 50 receives and waits for 50 completions in one call?
options: 50 with epoll, 50 with io_uring
51 with epoll, 1 with io_uring
2 with epoll, 2 with io_uring
51 with epoll, 51 with io_uring because each receive still enters the kernel
explain: epoll needs the `epoll_wait` plus one `read` per socket: 51. With io_uring the 50 requests are plain memory writes into the submission ring, and a single `io_uring_enter` submits them and waits for 50 completions. The receives still run in the kernel, but they no longer each need their own system call.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
question: A multishot recv posts a CQE with `res = -ENOBUFS` and no `IORING_CQE_F_MORE` flag. What should the server do?
options: Nothing: the recv stays armed and retries automatically
Close the socket, since ENOBUFS means the peer disconnected
Increase the SQ size
Return buffers to the provided buffer ring, then submit a new multishot recv for that socket
explain: The missing `F_MORE` says the multishot request has terminated, here because the buffer group ran dry. Replenish the ring (the app must keep returning consumed buffers) and re-arm the recv. The connection itself is fine.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
question: Which statement about cross-thread frees is correct?
options: mimalloc takes the owning thread's heap lock on every remote free
jemalloc returns a remotely freed object straight to its slab with no lock
All three forbid freeing memory allocated by another thread
tcmalloc's transfer cache lets objects freed on one CPU refill another CPU's cache without going through spans
explain: tcmalloc's transfer cache is a per-size-class array of pointers that one front-end fills and another drains. mimalloc uses a lock-free CAS onto the page's thread_free list. jemalloc caches the object in the freeing thread's tcache, then locks the owner's bin when flushing.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
question: In the `:majorities-ring` partition on five nodes, what does each node see?
options: Only itself
Exactly two neighbors plus itself, a majority, and a different majority from every other node
All four other nodes, but with delay
Two nodes in the minority and three in the majority, cleanly split
explain: Each node keeps links to its two ring neighbors, so it sees 3 of 5 nodes. That is a majority, but the majorities overlap rather than coincide, so connectivity is not transitive, a case that clean splits never exercise.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
question: You have a 1200-config space and time for 50 trials per shape. Which plan has the best expected outcome?
options: Grid search over the first 50 configs in enumeration order
Hill climb from one random start for all 50 trials
Rank all 1200 with a rough cost model, then measure the top 50
Measure 50 random configs 3 times each, with only 16 distinct configs tried
explain: A model only has to rank well, not predict exact times. In the simulation a model with roughly 2x error reaches 100 percent of the optimum by 50 measured candidates, while random reaches about 84 percent and a single hill climb about 84 percent. Enumeration order is an arbitrary slice of the space, and spending the budget on repeats of fewer configs is the right move only when the candidates are within noise of each other.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Poll-mode drivers: descriptor rings, doorbells and bursts
question: A new driver checks for received packets by reading the NIC's head register on every poll. What is the main problem?
options: Each read is a PCIe round trip, while the done flag in the descriptor is already in the CPU cache
Nothing; it is the standard method
Reading the head register disables DMA
The head register is only valid after an interrupt
explain: MMIO reads stall the core for a full trip across PCIe. Checking the done flag written by DMA into the last-level cache is far cheaper; drivers only write the tail register, once per burst.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
question: Same chain, but at inference (dropout disabled, so no mask and no dropout kernel). What is the bandwidth-model speedup from fusing scale, shift and GELU?
options: 3x
4x
explain: Eager: three kernels at 4N bytes each = 12N. Fused: read x (2N) and write the output (2N) = 4N. 12N / 4N = 3x.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
question: In Hinton et al.'s speech experiment, a model trained with soft targets on 3% of the data nearly matched one trained on 100% with hard labels. What best explains this?
options: Each soft target carries information about every class, so one example teaches far more than a one-hot label
Soft targets contain the correct labels for the other 97% of the data
Soft targets remove the need for a loss function on the student
The student had more parameters than the teacher
explain: A one-hot label says only which class is right. A soft target also says how plausible each wrong class is, which encodes what the teacher learned from the full dataset. That extra information per example, plus lower-variance gradients, acts as a strong regularizer, so the small subset goes much further.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
question: You distill a ResNet student from a ResNet-18 teacher and then from a much larger, more accurate teacher. The student does worse with the larger teacher. Which next step is supported by the research in this lesson?
options: Distill through an intermediate teacher assistant, or use an early-stopped teacher
Use an even larger teacher so the soft targets are more accurate
Drop the soft targets and train only on hard labels
Raise T to 100 so the targets become uniform
explain: This is the capacity-gap failure described by Cho and Hariharan and by Mirzadeh et al. Both an intermediate-size teacher assistant and an early-stopped (less sharp, easier to mimic) teacher are reported fixes. A larger teacher makes the gap worse.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
question: In the toy, per-channel 2-bit keys reached MSE 0.026 while per-token 4-bit keys reached 0.028. What does this suggest?
options: Bit width matters more than grouping axis
Choosing the right axis can matter as much as two extra bits
The toy is broken, since 4 bits must always win
Outlier channels only matter for values
explain: With the right grouping, 2 bits matched what per-token needed 4 bits for, because the range of each group no longer includes the outlier. 4 bits does not win automatically when its groups mix scales.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
question: A server runs Llama 3 8B with 40 GB of HBM free for KV and serves 200 users who each come back every few minutes with a growing 8K-token chat history. Without offloading, what happens on most return visits?
options: Prefix caching hits, because vLLM never evicts blocks that another request might reuse
The history was evicted from HBM (only about 37 such histories fit), so prefill recomputes it
The attention kernel reads the history directly from CPU memory over PCIe
The request is rejected until enough HBM is freed
explain: 200 histories of 1 GiB each cannot fit in 40 GB; only about 37 can. Free blocks are evicted when space is needed, so most returning users miss and pay a full prefill. Offloading to a 512 GB DRAM tier would keep all 200 histories.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
question: An engineer configures an offload store whose keys are the hash of the token IDs only. They then deploy a new fine-tuned version of the model behind the same store. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: KV depends only on the tokens
Every lookup misses because the hashes change
Hits return KV computed by the old weights, silently corrupting outputs
The store evicts all old entries automatically on deploy
explain: K and V are projections of hidden states through the model's weights, so different weights give different KV for the same tokens. Keys must include the model identity (and dtype, adapter, and similar), or stale KV is served as a hit.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node at (10, 3) receives a message stamped (8, 7) when its physical clock reads 9. What is the result?
explain: l = max(10, 8, 9) = 10 equals only the old l, so c = 3 + 1 = 4, giving (10, 4). The message's counter 7 is ignored because its l is smaller: (8, 7) is already less than (10, 3). Taking max(c, cm) + 1 here would be a bug that inflates c.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: ColBERTv2 distills a cross-encoder with a KL-divergence loss over a 64-way score distribution instead of regressing the cross-encoder's raw scores with mean squared error. What is the reason the paper gives?
options: KL divergence is cheaper to compute than MSE
ColBERT's scores (sums of cosines) have a restricted scale that may not line up with the cross-encoder's output scale; KL compares the distributions over passages instead
MSE cannot be backpropagated through a max operation
The cross-encoder only outputs binary labels
explain: A sum of 32 cosines lives in a fixed range, while a cross-encoder's logits can be on any scale. Matching softmax distributions over the same 64 passages only asks ColBERT to rank them the same way, which is what retrieval needs.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: Why does writing reasoning tokens let a fixed-depth transformer solve problems it cannot solve in one pass?
options: Generated tokens are fed back as inputs, so later passes can build on earlier results, increasing effective serial depth
Longer outputs give the attention softmax a sharper distribution
Each written token adds new trainable parameters at inference
The KV cache stores the answer before it is written
explain: Each pass has bounded depth L. Feeding outputs back chains passes together, so n written steps allow roughly n x L layers of sequential computation. Coconut keeps this feedback loop but passes a vector instead of a token.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: Using the same line and bounds (min_err = -1, max_err = +1), you look up key 30, which is not stored. f(30) = 5.41. Which positions do you search, and what lower_bound do you return?
options: Positions 4 to 6; the first key >= 30 is not there, so return not found
Positions 4 to 6; return position 6, the last slot in the window, which holds 26
Only position 5, because the error bound is for stored keys
Positions 4 to 6, then continue right: 41 at position 7 is the lower_bound
explain: The prediction rounds to 5, so the window is 4 to 6, holding 21, 24 and 26, all smaller than 30. The answer sits just past the window edge at position 7. Bounds measured on stored keys say nothing certain about absent keys, so when the search ends at a window boundary you must extend it. Kraska et al. describe exactly this fix.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: Your service stores immutable sorted files that are rewritten by background compaction, and lookups are read-heavy. Which learned index design fits most naturally?
options: An ALEX-style updatable index, because data changes over time
A one-pass, error-bounded index (RadixSpline or PGM-style) rebuilt during each compaction
A single deep neural network trained once and never retrained
None: learned indexes cannot be used with files on disk
explain: Each file is written once in sorted order and then never modified, so the model never goes stale for that file. A single-pass build during the merge costs little extra, which is exactly the argument the RadixSpline paper makes for LSM trees.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPS regularizer
question: Two terms have the same weight 0.3 in a document. Term A appears in 1 document of the batch, term B in all of them with similar weights. Under FLOPS, which weight is pushed toward zero faster?
options: A, because rare terms are noise
Both equally, since the weights are equal
B, because its mean weight across the batch is larger, so its gradient 2 a_j / N is larger
Neither; FLOPS only acts on queries
explain: The FLOPS gradient for a weight is proportional to the term's batch mean. B is active everywhere, so its posting list is long and its push is strong. L1 would treat A and B the same.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: A pair is correctly ordered with a gap of 6 (sigma = 1). Roughly how big is its push?
options: About 0.0025, close to zero
About 0.5
About 1, the maximum
Exactly 0
explain: Push = 1 / (1 + e^6) = 0.0025. Well-separated, correctly ordered pairs contribute almost nothing, so RankNet focuses on misordered or close pairs. It never reaches exactly 0.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: A head has $d_k=64$. A prompt states 500 different key facts, each with its own key direction. What happens to recall under plain linear attention?
options: Nothing, because 500 tokens is short
Keys cannot all be orthogonal in 64 dimensions, so reads mix many stored values
Only the last 64 facts are kept and older ones are cleanly deleted
The model switches to softmax attention automatically
explain: At most 64 directions can be mutually orthogonal. With 500 associations the overlaps $k_i^\top k_j$ are nonzero and every read returns a weighted mixture. Nothing is cleanly deleted either: additive memory never forgets.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: A team has 2,000 queries and 40 ranker variants per week, and wants NDCG@10 for all of them. What is the main reason they consider an LLM judge?
options: NDCG cannot be computed from human labels
Each new variant surfaces unjudged documents, and human labels for all of them are too slow and costly
LLM labels are always more accurate than human labels
LLMs can compute NDCG directly without labels
explain: NDCG needs a grade for every returned document. New rankers keep surfacing unjudged documents, so the labelling bill grows with every experiment. The LLM judge makes that bill small. Accuracy is not automatic: it has to be checked against gold labels.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: A colleague adds an "include more detail" step to the generator in a RAG system, and the LLM judge's preference for its answers rises from 50% to 70%. Which explanation should you rule out before celebrating?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge may be rewarding length rather than better content
Position bias in the generator
Kendall's tau is too low
The gold set is too large
explain: Zheng et al.'s repetitive list attack shows weaker judges preferring padded answers over 90% of the time. Check with length-controlled comparisons or human spot checks before attributing the gain to quality.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Which mitigation targets position bias specifically?
options: Using a judge from a different model family
Fitting a tanh length term
Evaluating both orders and combining the results
Adding a reference answer to the prompt
explain: Balanced Position Calibration (Wang et al.) and swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) run both orders so that position effects cancel or show up as ties. A different-family judge targets self-preference; the length term targets verbosity.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
question: An email assistant reads the user's inbox and can send emails. Which threat is the most direct route to it sending data to an attacker?
options: A jailbreak typed by the user
Hallucinated claims in a summary
Indirect prompt injection in an incoming email
A slow model response
explain: The attacker only needs to send an email: the assistant reads it as context, and injected instructions plus a send-email tool give a path to exfiltration. A user jailbreak needs the user to be the attacker; hallucination does not move data out.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A vendor reports their jailbreak detector blocks 99% of attacks in a public benchmark. What is the most important question before relying on it?
options: Which GPU it runs on
Whether it uses a transformer
How it performs against adaptive attacks crafted against it, and what its false positive rate is on your traffic
Whether the benchmark is in English
explain: Static benchmarks measure known attacks. Studies such as Zou et al. and Hackett et al. show optimized or obfuscated inputs evade guards, and the FPR on your own base rate decides how many real users get blocked.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: Paging lets a server admit a request after allocating only its prompt's blocks. What new problem does this create that max-length reservation did not have?
options: Requests can no longer share a batch
The pool can run out in the middle of generation, when running requests need new blocks that are not there
Prompts longer than one block cannot be stored
Block tables use more memory than the KV cache itself
explain: Reservation guaranteed every admitted request could finish. Allocating on demand bets that not everyone will grow at once; when the bet loses, some running request has nowhere to put its next token. Handling that is the job of preemption, the next lesson.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: With manual chain-of-thought, your code needs only the final number. What does Anthropic suggest?
options: Ask for the answer first, then the reasoning
Forbid reasoning so the output is just the number
Ask for reasoning first and the final answer inside <answer> tags, then extract the tags
Parse the last number that appears anywhere in the response
explain: Reasoning first keeps the benefit; a fixed delimiter makes extraction reliable. Answer-first loses the benefit, and grabbing the last number breaks as soon as the model mentions a number after its answer.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
question: LangChain's default few-shot prompt includes the question *What are songs that were not published on Spotify* for a data source whose only fields are artist, length and genre. What filter does the example answer give?
options: and(ne("platform", "Spotify"))
NO_FILTER, because no field records the platform
not(contain("artist", "Spotify"))
It refuses to answer the query
explain: The example answer is query "" with filter NO_FILTER. The prompt also instructs the model that filters may only refer to attributes that exist. Inventing a platform field would produce a query the store cannot run, or one that silently matches nothing.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: To benefit from prompt prefix caching, where should the user's query go in the parser prompt?
options: At the end, after the instructions, field descriptions and examples
At the start, so the model reads it first
In the middle, between instructions and examples
It does not matter, caching hashes the whole prompt
explain: Caching reuses a matching prefix, so everything identical across requests should come first and the part that changes every time should come last. A query at the start changes the prefix on every request and nothing is reused.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: Why does the relative saving of FIRST shrink when passages get longer?
options: Longer passages make the first-token logits less accurate
FIRST must generate more tokens for long passages
Prefill grows with L while the decode time saved stays the same, so the saved share falls
Long passages force smaller windows
explain: The saved part is (t_id m - 1) x TPOT, which does not depend on L. Prefill, which both methods pay, grows with mL.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Two passages get p(Yes) = 0.83 and 0.79 from separate calls. Why might the lower one still be the better passage?
options: Each score is produced in isolation, so small differences reflect calibration noise rather than a real comparison
p(Yes) is always inversely related to relevance
Sorting requires scores to sum to 1
The second call used fewer tokens
explain: The model never saw the two passages side by side. Its probability depends on passage length, wording and prompt quirks, so a 0.04 gap is not a reliable comparison. Pairwise and listwise prompts address exactly this.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Why did RankGPT's distilled 440M DeBERTa reranker beat its ChatGPT teacher on BEIR?
options: It was trained on human relevance labels as well
It ranks each passage with a stable deterministic score instead of an occasionally malformed or inconsistent permutation
It used a longer context window than ChatGPT
It reranked 1000 passages instead of 100
explain: The student learns the teacher's preferences through a pairwise RankNet loss but scores each passage with a deterministic forward pass, so it avoids the teacher's missing ids, repetitions and window-to-window inconsistency. The authors attribute the gap to this stability.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
question: After launching in Japan, your router's share of strong-model calls drops from 35% to 12% and complaints about answer quality rise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The strong model became cheaper
Input distribution shift: the router misjudges the difficulty of prompts unlike its training data and sends hard ones to the weak model
Judge bias toward longer answers
The router's GPU is overloaded
explain: A sudden change in routing mix plus worse quality right after new traffic arrives points to drift. Bedrock's docs say its routing is optimized only for English prompts, and RouteLLM's routers fell to near random on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: Inlier ratio is 0.5 and you need 99% confidence. How many RANSAC iterations does a homography (s = 4) need?
explain: N = log(0.01)/log(1 - 0.5^4) = log(0.01)/log(0.9375) = 71.36, rounded up to 72. 16 is 1/w^4, the expected number of draws to see the first clean sample, which is not enough for 99% confidence. 567 is the answer for w = 0.3.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: A thread in enqueue reads Tail = X and finds X.next is not NULL. What does the algorithm do?
options: Wait until the thread that linked X.next swings Tail
Try to CAS Tail forward to X.next, then retry its own enqueue
Link its node after X anyway
Return failure because the queue is full
explain: That is E13: Tail is lagging, so the thread helps advance it and loops. Waiting would make the algorithm blocking, and linking after X would break the list because X is not the last node.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Why is "88 percent of Thunderbird's templates are missing from a 2,000-line sample" a problem for a hand-written regex set, but not fatal for a template miner?
options: The miner has already seen all 1,241 templates during training
The miner stores raw lines, so it can re-derive templates on demand
The miner creates a new template group the first time it sees an unmatched line, so unseen formats cost nothing extra
Rare templates are noise and a miner correctly discards them
explain: An online miner's whole job is to open a new group for a line that matches nothing. A regex set has to be edited by a person before the new format parses at all, and until then those lines fall into an unparsed bucket. Rare templates are usually the valuable ones: error-level messages are rare by construction.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: Your log volume quadruples and the parser falls behind. Which of the Huawei deployment's four measures gives both a throughput win and an accuracy win?
options: Partitioning by verbosity level and component, since different levels and components come from different logging statements: fewer candidates per partition, and the partitions parse in parallel
Raising the similarity threshold so fewer comparisons are needed
Reducing the tree depth to shorten every walk
Sampling one line in four and extrapolating the counts
explain: Partitioning narrows the search space, which speeds parsing, and it also removes the chance of merging templates across components, which helps accuracy. It is also the parallelization key they used with Spark. Threshold and depth are accuracy trade-offs, not free wins, and sampling destroys exactly the rare error templates you most want to count.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: You move a Ring Attention job from NVLink (300 GB/s) to a 25 GB/s network with the same GPUs (312 TFLOP/s). Roughly what minimum block size now hides communication?
options: 1,040 tokens, unchanged since hidden size cancels
About 87 tokens
About 12,480 tokens
It can never be hidden on a slower link
explain: c >= F / B = 312e12 / 25e9 = 12,480. Bandwidth dropped 12x, so the minimum block grows 12x. The hidden size cancels, but the bandwidth does not.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
question: A colleague simplifies the design: set s0 = e and stop feeding e into later iterations. What does the paper's reasoning predict?
options: Nothing changes, because e is already inside s0
The loop becomes less stable: its end point depends on the starting point, not on continued use of the input
Training becomes cheaper and generalizes better because the adapter is removed
The model becomes a Universal Transformer and gains Turing completeness
explain: The authors argue the input must be injected at every step, as data enters every step of gradient descent. With e only in the initial state, the iteration cannot behave like a stable, input-dependent operator; its result depends on the boundary condition.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
question: A colleague initializes both A and B to zero to be extra safe. What happens during training?
options: Training proceeds normally but more slowly
A learns first, then B
The update stays exactly zero, because each matrix's gradient is multiplied by the other matrix
The model diverges because the scale alpha/r is applied to zeros
explain: The gradient for B contains Ax and the gradient for A contains B. With both at zero, both gradients are zero at every step, so nothing ever changes. That is why one of the two must be random.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: Your LoRA r = 16 on attention only underperforms full fine-tuning on a code instruction set. Which change is most supported by the evidence in this course?
options: Lower the learning rate by 10x
Switch to adapting only Wq
Target all linear layers including the MLP and raise the rank
Initialize B randomly instead of to zero
explain: QLoRA needed all linear layers to match full fine-tuning, and Biderman et al. found MLP modules drive most gains and that code needs high ranks. Their recommendation was a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, not lower.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: Unlearned model A uses a small learning rate plus a retain loss and keeps 95% of its utility. Model B used plain gradient ascent and collapsed to near-zero utility. After 4-bit quantization, which is more likely to reveal the forgotten knowledge again?
options: A, because its small weight changes mostly fall inside the same quantization bins as the original weights
B, because gradient ascent changes few weights
Neither, quantization only reduces precision and cannot restore information
Both equally, quantization resets every model to the original
explain: Quantization maps every weight within half a step of a grid point to the same value. Utility-preserving unlearning moves weights by tiny amounts, so the quantized unlearned model is nearly the quantized original, which still knows the facts. Zhang et al. saw 21% retained knowledge rise to 83% at 4 bits; GA was the exception only because it had wrecked the model.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
question: In the 64-objects-per-page model, a workload frees 95% of its objects at random. What fraction of pages becomes returnable?
options: About 95%
About 3.8%
About 50%
Exactly 0%
explain: A page is empty only if all 64 objects died: 0.95^64 is about 0.0375, so about 3.8% of pages. The other 96% each hold at least one survivor and stay resident. Correlated lifetimes in real programs do better than this random model.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: A spin lock is implemented as `while LOCKED.swap(true, Acquire) {}` ... critical section ... `LOCKED.store(false, ORD)`. Which ORD is the weakest correct choice?
options: Relaxed
Acquire
SeqCst, because unlocking must be globally visible
Release
explain: The unlock must publish the critical section's writes to the next locker. That needs a Release store paired with the Acquire swap. Acquire is not even allowed on a plain store, Relaxed creates no happens-before, and SeqCst works but promises far more than needed.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: A developer removes the re-validation step: after `hp[me] = t; full_fence();` the code reads `t->next` directly. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the fence already makes the hazard pointer visible
Another thread may have retired and freed t before the hazard pointer was published, so reading its next field touches freed memory
The CAS will always fail
The retired list will grow without bound
explain: Publishing only protects a node that is still in the structure at the moment the slot becomes visible. If t was unlinked and a scan ran between the load and the publish, the scan saw no slot and freed t. The re-read proves t was still reachable after the publish, so every later scan must see the slot.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A Rust program uses crossbeam-epoch. Memory grows steadily, and a profiler shows one thread blocked on a channel receive inside a function that holds an `epoch::Guard`. What fixes it?
options: Increase the bag size from 64
Drop the guard (or call repin) before blocking on the channel
Switch the CAS to SeqCst ordering
Call `pin()` more often on other threads
explain: The blocked thread stays pinned in an old epoch, so the global epoch cannot advance past it and every thread's garbage waits. Bag size and memory ordering do not change that. Holding guards only for short, non-blocking sections is the rule for any grace-period scheme.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: System X ranks a query's 10 true matches at positions 1, 40, 41, ..., 48. System Y ranks them at positions 2 to 11. Which statement is right?
options: X has the better rank-1 and the better AP
Both have the same AP because both find all 10 matches
Y has the better rank-1, X the better AP
X has the better rank-1, but Y has a much better AP
explain: X's first match is at position 1, so rank-1 is a hit for X and a miss for Y. But X buries 9 matches around position 40, so its precision at those hits is low. AP is about 0.22 for X and 0.80 for Y. AP rewards finding all instances early, which is why Market-1501 reports mAP.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
question: Version X averages 102 ns with 95% interval [98, 106]. Version Y averages 100 ns with interval [97, 103]. What should you conclude?
options: Y is 2% faster; ship it
X is faster because its interval is wider
Compare the fastest runs instead
The data do not show a difference; reduce noise or take more runs before deciding
explain: The intervals overlap heavily, so a 2 ns gap is within what noise produces. Width says how uncertain the mean is, not which version is faster. The best-of approach is the misleading method that Georges et al. warn against.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A token has rollout logprob -2.30 and trainer logprob -1.40, so r is about 2.46. What weight does it get under TIS with the default interval, and under clip-or-pop?
options: TIS 2.46, clip-or-pop 2.0
TIS 1.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 2.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 0, clip-or-pop 2.0
explain: TIS clamps r to [0, 2] and keeps the clamped value, so the token is damped to 2.0. Clip-or-pop zeroes the weight of any token outside the interval, so it is dropped. Tokens inside the interval keep their unclipped r under both.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
question: Spot the bug: to save build time, a team computes each leaf's min and max error on a 10% random sample of its keys, then searches only that window at lookup time.
options: Nothing breaks; sampling only makes the bounds slightly loose
Lookups get slower but always remain correct
Some stored keys can fall outside the window and lookups for them will wrongly report not found
The routing in stage 0 stops working
explain: The guarantee comes from checking every stored key. A key outside the sample can have a larger error than any sampled key, so a search limited to the window misses it. Either compute bounds on all keys (one pass, cheap) or search outward with exponential search, which needs no bounds.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
question: Why didn't DeepSeek simply use MQA, which has an even smaller cache than MLA?
options: MQA cannot be used with a KV cache
In their 7B ablation MQA lost clearly to MHA on hard benchmarks, and they wanted MHA-level quality
MQA needs more GPU memory for weights
MQA does not support causal masking
explain: DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.1 shows MQA at 37.9 MMLU vs 45.2 for MHA at 7B. MLA was designed to get a small cache without paying that quality cost.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: For a long prompt's prefill, why does vLLM up-project the latents into full keys and values instead of using the absorbed path?
options: The absorbed path gives different numerical results
Prefill does not use a KV cache
Prefill is compute-bound, and the absorbed path does more FLOPs per score (576-wide vs 192-wide dot products), while its memory savings matter little there
RoPE cannot be applied during prefill
explain: Both paths compute the same function. The absorbed form wins when reading the cache dominates (decode); the plain multi-head form wins when arithmetic dominates (prefill).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
question: Why did S-LoRA put adapter weights and KV cache in one paged pool instead of two separate pools?
options: Because both are stacks of H-sized vectors that come and go dynamically, so sharing H-sized pages avoids fragmentation and lets the split between them change with load
Because adapters and KV cache are always the same size
Because the base model weights also need paging
Because PCIe transfers require page-aligned buffers
explain: A KV tensor is (S, H) and a LoRA weight is (R, H). With pages of one H-vector each, both fit the same allocator, holes left by one can be reused by the other, and the balance shifts automatically between many adapters and long contexts.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: Your index stores 3 chunks per web page. Fusion is keyed by chunk id and the top-5 after RRF holds 3 chunks of the same page. What is the most direct fix?
options: Fuse by source document id (or collapse chunks of one page) before truncating to 5
Raise k from 60 to 600
Generate more paraphrases
Switch from RRF to an unranked union
explain: The slots are being spent on near-duplicates of one source. Keying fusion or a post-fusion collapse by source id frees slots for other documents. Changing k or adding phrasings does not address what counts as a duplicate.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Under Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model, you double k0 from 500 to 1000 in a BM25 plus monoBERT pipeline. What happens to monoBERT's cost per query?
options: It stays the same, because monoBERT runs once per query
It grows by about log 2
It roughly doubles, because cost is unit cost times the number of documents scored
It quadruples
explain: monoBERT scores each candidate independently, so its cost is U x k0. Nogueira et al. report exactly this: latency increases linearly with the number of candidates, while quality shows diminishing returns.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Your LLM listwise reranker on the top 100 meets quality targets but costs too much per query. Which change follows the cascade principle best?
options: Run the LLM on the top 100 but with a random initial order to avoid bias
Drop stage 1 and let the LLM read the whole corpus in windows
Let a distilled cross-encoder rerank the 100 and send only its top 20 to the LLM in one window
Increase the step size to 20 so windows no longer overlap
explain: Put the cheap model where the list is long and the expensive model where it is short: one LLM window instead of 9 calls. RankGPT's own GPT-4-on-top-30 result follows the same pattern. Random initial order hurt in the paper, and s = w removes the overlap that carries good passages forward.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: An MTP model with one extra draft has acceptance rate 0.9. Under the simplified independence model, about how many tokens does each forward pass yield, and why is the measured speedup lower?
options: 1.9 tokens; verification passes cost a little more than plain decode steps
2.0 tokens; the draft is always accepted at greedy temperature
1.81 tokens, because 0.9 squared is 0.81
1.9 tokens; the speedup is lower because outputs differ from greedy decoding
explain: Expected tokens = 1 + a = 1.9. The wall-clock gain is smaller because each verifying pass processes extra positions and runs the drafter. Output does not differ: greedy verification reproduces greedy decoding exactly. DeepSeek-V3 reports 85% to 90% acceptance and 1.8x tokens per second.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: Why does SOAP lose less than Shampoo when eigenvectors are recomputed only every 100 steps?
options: SOAP uses a more accurate eigensolver than Shampoo
SOAP keeps updating Adam's second moment every step in the slowly changing basis, while Shampoo's preconditioner is frozen between refreshes
SOAP does not use L and R at all
SOAP uses a larger learning rate that hides the staleness
explain: Both compute their expensive rotation or roots rarely. Between refreshes Shampoo applies a fixed preconditioner (grafting adapts only a scalar per layer), whereas SOAP's $V$ keeps tracking per-coordinate scale. The paper's explanation is exactly this continual second-moment update in the current basis.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Which of these is a vector-like parameter in a Transformer whose width is d_model?
options: A LayerNorm gain vector of length d_model
The query projection W_q (d_model x d_model)
The MLP up-projection (d_model x 4 d_model)
A scalar temperature applied to the logits
explain: A LayerNorm gain has exactly one dimension that grows with width, so it is vector-like and keeps a constant Adam LR. W_q and the MLP matrices have two infinite dimensions (matrix-like). A scalar has none, so it is scalar-like and held constant.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
question: Your critical sections take about 50 ns, but the machine runs 32 threads on 8 cores. Should you use a pure spin lock in user space?
options: Yes: 50 ns is shorter than any system call
No: with more threads than cores, holders get preempted, and spinners can then burn whole time slices
Yes, as long as the spin loop calls spin_loop()
No: spin locks do not work with more than 8 threads
explain: Short critical sections are only half of the condition. With 32 threads on 8 cores the holder is often not running, and a spinner cannot make it run. A spin-then-sleep mutex handles the short case nearly as well and the preempted case far better.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
question: Under PostgreSQL MVCC, transaction W runs UPDATE on row R and has not committed yet. Transaction X now runs UPDATE on the same row R. What happens to X?
options: X proceeds immediately and writes its own version next to W's
X waits until W commits or rolls back
X reads W's uncommitted value and overwrites it
X fails instantly with a serialization error
explain: MVCC removes reader versus writer blocking only. Two writers on the same row still conflict, so X waits for W to finish. What X does afterward depends on the isolation level, which lesson 3 covers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
question: Autovacuum runs every few minutes on a busy table, yet the table keeps growing and its dead-tuple count never drops. What is the most likely cause?
options: autovacuum_freeze_max_age is set too low
HOT updates are disabled by the fillfactor
A session that opened a transaction hours ago and is still idle in it
The table has too many indexes
explain: Dead tuples are removable only when no snapshot can see them. An old open transaction holds back that horizon for the whole database, so VACUUM runs but has to keep the versions. End the session and the next VACUUM can clean up.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
question: Why is the Viterbi table 3 tokens by 3 labels rather than a list of 27 sequence scores?
options: Because the emissions are independent of each other
Because the transition matrix is symmetric, so half the sequences are duplicates
Because the score only couples adjacent labels, so the best prefix ending in a given label can be reused by every extension of it
Because Viterbi is an approximation that prunes low-scoring sequences
explain: A linear-chain model has only bigram interactions, so for each label at each position the single best prefix ending there is all you ever need. Viterbi is exact, not an approximation, and that reuse is what turns an exponential count into n x |Y| x |Y| work.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: A model must copy the token that appeared 3 positions ago. Which NSA branch is designed to make this easy, and why is it a separate branch?
options: Compression, because it summarizes every token
Selection, because top-n scoring always ranks the most recent block first
Sliding window, because local patterns are learned fastest and a dedicated branch keeps them from shortcutting the long-range branches
None; NSA cannot attend to recent tokens exactly
explain: The window branch attends to the last $w$ tokens in full. The paper isolates it because local patterns adapt quickly and would otherwise dominate the learning signal of the compression and selection branches.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
question: Two 8-bit hashes are 10110010 and 10100110. What is their Hamming distance?
explain: XOR gives 00010100, which has two 1 bits, so the distance is 2. Only positions 3 and 5 (counting from 0 on the left) differ.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: A platform must catch reposts of a known image that users have cropped to a square and covered with a caption. Which approach fits best?
options: aHash with a looser threshold of 20
A learned copy descriptor such as SSCD with nearest neighbor search and verification
PDQ with all 8 dihedral hashes
SHA-256 of the decoded pixels
explain: Crops and overlays change what lands in each cell of a global hash, and PDQ's own documentation puts deep crops out of scope. Dihedral hashes only cover rotations and flips. SSCD is trained with crops and text overlays as augmentations, so copies under those edits stay close in its embedding space.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: You turn on `grpo.async_grpo.enabled: true` but leave `policy.generation.colocated.enabled: true` with the vLLM backend. What does the async guide say?
options: It works; async only changes the loss
Set max_trajectory_age_steps to 0 instead
Switch the training backend to Automodel
Disable colocated inference: async mode with vLLM needs dedicated generation resources
explain: Async mode overlaps generation and training, which cannot happen on GPUs that must take turns. The async guide lists disabling colocated inference as required for the vLLM backend.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: A service is started with `numactl --membind=0` on a 2-node box. Node 0 has 64 GiB, node 1 has 64 GiB, and the service grows to 80 GiB. What happens?
options: The extra 16 GiB is allocated on node 1 automatically
The kernel switches the process to interleave mode
Allocations that node 0 cannot satisfy fail, because bind never falls back to node 1
explain: MPOL_BIND restricts allocation to the listed nodes. numactl(8) says allocation will fail when there is not enough memory on them. If spilling to node 1 is acceptable, use --preferred=0 instead.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Why flash cannot overwrite a page in place
question: A drive uses a direct-mapped layout with 256 KB erase blocks of 4 KB pages. The host overwrites a single 4 KB page. How many page programs does the flash perform?
options: 1, because only one page changed
63, the other live pages
64, the whole block is rewritten after the erase
128, one read and one program per page
explain: After erasing, every page of the block is blank, so all 64 pages (63 preserved plus the new one) must be programmed. That is 64x more flash writing than the host asked for, and the block takes one more P/E cycle per host write.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: A host driver reaps completions by checking the phase tag. After the CQ wraps from the last slot back to slot 0, what must the driver do?
options: Nothing: new entries always have phase tag 1
Reset every phase tag in the queue to 0
Read the controller's CQ tail register
Flip the phase value it expects, because the controller now writes the opposite bit
explain: On each wrap the controller inverts the phase tag it writes. The host tracks the expected value and flips it when its head wraps. The CQ tail is internal to the controller and not visible to the host.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
question: You call `model.predict(img, conf=0.25, iou=0.7)` and see two boxes on one car with IoU 0.6 between them. Which change removes the duplicate?
options: Set iou=0.5 so NMS suppresses boxes overlapping by more than 0.5
Raise conf to 0.5
Set iou=0.9
Set max_det=1
explain: Here `iou` is the NMS threshold: boxes overlapping a higher-scoring box by more than it are removed. At 0.7 a 0.6 overlap survives; at 0.5 it is suppressed. Raising conf might drop the duplicate only if its score is low, and max_det=1 would discard every other car too.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Keeping object storage off the hot read path
question: In Neon, why does a COMMIT not include the latency of an object storage PUT?
options: Postgres batches commits for up to a second
Durability comes from a majority of safekeepers storing the WAL; pages reach object storage later, off the commit path
The compute node's local NVMe is replicated
Object storage writes are done with S3 Express One Zone
explain: Neon defines commit as WAL acknowledged by a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver materializes pages and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. If a safekeeper dies, the quorum continues; if the pageserver dies, its state is rebuilt from WAL and object storage.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
question: Which setup guarantees a complete trace for every request that returned a 500?
options: Tail sampling in the collector, which buffers a trace's spans and decides once they are complete
Head sampling at 1 in 10 plus a longer retention period
A trace-id ratio sampler at 0.01, since its decision is deterministic
Setting the sampled bit at the gateway only when the gateway sees an error
explain: Only a decision made after the spans exist can condition on the error. Longer retention keeps dropped spans dropped. A deterministic ratio sampler is still a ratio. The last option fails because the gateway must inject traceparent before the request runs, so at decision time the error has not happened yet, and the downstream spans would already have been dropped.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Scoring OCR output: edit distance, CER and WER
question: You must pick one metric to decide whether an invoice-total extractor is good enough for automatic payment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Average CER over all page text
Average WER over all page text
Exact match of the normalized total field per document
Detection F-score of text boxes
explain: Payment needs the exact amount. Page-level CER can look excellent while the one field that matters has a wrong digit. Field-level exact match after agreed normalization measures what the business cares about.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
question: Library `img` uses libpng only inside img.cpp; its public header img.h never mentions png types. Which line is right?
options: target_link_libraries(img PUBLIC PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img INTERFACE PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img PRIVATE PNG::PNG)
include_directories(/usr/include/libpng) at the top level
explain: Only the implementation uses libpng, so PRIVATE. PUBLIC would leak png's include paths and definitions to every consumer; INTERFACE would not give them to img.cpp itself, so img would fail to compile. A global include_directories bypasses targets entirely.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: Your PR shows `test (windows-latest)` failed and `test (ubuntu-latest)` and `test (macos-latest)` cancelled. What do you know about Linux and macOS?
options: They passed, because only Windows is marked as failed
They also failed, because cancelled means failed
Nothing yet: with the default fail-fast, GitHub cancelled them when Windows failed
They were skipped because they need the Windows job
explain: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to true and cancels in-progress and queued matrix jobs when any one fails. Cancelled jobs did not finish, so they give no information. Fix the Windows failure or set `fail-fast: false` to see all results.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: Which situation lets a reviewer withhold approval even if the code is clean and well tested?
options: The reviewer would have used a different but equally valid algorithm
The author used tabs where the style guide is silent and the file already uses tabs
The PR adds a feature the project has decided it does not want
The PR is 40 lines and the reviewer expected 30
explain: Google's guide explicitly allows denying a feature the maintainers do not want in their system, however well designed. An equally valid alternative should defer to the author, consistency with the existing file is correct, and line counts alone are not a reason.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: A reviewer in another time zone sees that only two typo fixes remain. The author will be asleep for the next 10 hours. What does Google's guide suggest?
options: Request changes so the author fixes the typos, then review again tomorrow
Wait to approve until the typos are fixed, to keep the process strict
Approve with comments (LGTM with comments), noting the typos to fix before merging
Fix the typos and approve your own commit
explain: Minor remaining comments are exactly the case for LGTM with comments, and the guide calls it especially worth considering across time zones. Requesting another round costs the author a full extra day for two typos.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Which action breaks the Linux kernel's guidance for AI coding assistants?
options: Adding an Assisted-by tag
Letting the assistant add a Signed-off-by line to the commit
Writing a reproducer before sending a bug fix
Stating in the changelog which tool found the bug
explain: Only humans can legally certify the DCO, so AI agents must not add Signed-off-by. The human submitter reviews the code, adds their own sign-off and takes responsibility. The other three are things the guidance asks for.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: Why does a plain `git push` fail right after a successful `git rebase upstream/main` on a branch you had already pushed?
options: The pushed commits were rewritten, so the remote tip is no longer an ancestor of your local tip
Rebase deletes the remote branch
GitHub blocks pushes to branches that have an open PR
Rebase changes the remote URL of origin
explain: Without force, git push only accepts fast-forward updates. Rebasing replaced your commits with new ones, so the old remote tip is no longer in your branch's history. Pushing to a branch with an open PR is normal and updates the PR.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: Which pair can be combined into one distributed program?
options: GPL-2.0-only code inside a GPL-3.0-only project
MIT code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
GPL-3.0 code inside an Apache-2.0 project that stays Apache-2.0
Apache-2.0 code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
explain: MIT is GPL-compatible: its only condition is keeping the notice, which any GPL version allows. The other three either mix incompatible GPL versions, need the whole to become GPL, or add restrictions GPLv2 forbids.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: Why does benchstat's documentation recommend interleaving before and after runs?
options: It makes each individual run faster
Go benchmarks crash when run in blocks
So that slow changes in the machine (heat, background jobs) hit both versions evenly instead of only one
Because the U test requires alternating samples
explain: Noise must be spread evenly across both versions. In blocked order, any drift during the session is attributed entirely to whichever version ran later.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
question: Plain git blame says every line of a function was last changed by a commit titled "Run formatter". What is the most useful next command?
options: `git log -1` on that commit and conclude its author wrote the function
`git blame --reverse file`
`git grep -p` on the function name
`git blame -w --ignore-rev <formatter-hash> file` to look past the formatting commit
explain: A formatting commit is the last modifier but not the author of the logic. Ignoring whitespace and the formatter commit points each line at the commit that changed its content. --reverse answers a different question: the last revision in which a line still existed.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
question: You give a reducer an interestingness test that returns success whenever the compiler exits with a non-zero code. The output is a tiny file that triggers a syntax error. What went wrong?
options: The reducer has a bug; delta debugging should never produce invalid input
The test was not specific: a syntax error is also a non-zero exit, so the reducer drifted to a different, trivial failure
The input was too large for delta debugging to handle
The test should have returned non-zero for interesting candidates
explain: Reducers keep whatever the test calls interesting. "Any non-zero exit" includes syntax errors, which are trivially easy to keep, so reduction slides toward them. Grep for the exact crash message or assertion so only the original bug counts.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
question: A 5-commit series has commit 3 that does not compile (it was fixed in commit 4). Why might a maintainer ask you to fix this before merging with a merge commit?
options: Because git bisect may land on commit 3 and be unable to test it, hiding which commit introduced a later bug
Because CI only tests the first commit
Because GitHub refuses to merge a PR with a broken commit
Because commit 3 doubles the review time
explain: A merge commit keeps every commit on the main branch. Bisect can check out any of them; an untestable commit must be skipped, and if it is next to the culprit, git cannot say which one is first bad.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
question: Why does vLLM evict all of a sequence's blocks at once instead of picking the least recently used blocks like an OS?
options: Every decode step attends over all of the sequence's earlier tokens, so a partially evicted sequence cannot run anyway
GPU memory only supports freeing whole requests
LRU needs timestamps that GPUs cannot record
Partial eviction would break the block size invariant
explain: Attention reads every previous token's KV, so a sequence with any block missing cannot take its next step. The paper therefore evicts all or none of a sequence's blocks, and gang-schedules sequences that share blocks, such as beam candidates.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
question: In a flame graph, `json_encode` is 300 px wide but the boxes on top of it cover 290 px. What does that tell you?
options: json_encode itself is the hot spot; optimize its loop
json_encode was called 300 times
Almost all of json_encode's time is in the functions it calls; it executes very little itself
json_encode ran during the first quarter of the profile
explain: Only the exposed top edge (10 px) is self time. The other 290 px belong to its callees. Width says nothing about call counts, and x position says nothing about when.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
question: Spot the bug: `n->key = k; n->next = old; clwb(n); head = n; clwb(&head); sfence();` (n fits in one line; head is in another line).
options: Nothing: the final sfence orders everything before it
CLWB should be CLFLUSH, because CLWB keeps the line in cache so it is not durable
The sfence must come between clwb(n) and head = n; otherwise head can be durable before the node
head must be written with a non-temporal store
explain: The single trailing fence only guarantees both lines are durable at the end. Before it, head = n may be evicted or written back first, giving the head-only crash state. CLWB keeping a clean copy in cache is fine: the data was written back.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
question: A colleague says: "`char buf[8]; int *p = (int *)(buf + 1); *p = 7;` is fine on x86 because x86 allows unaligned loads." What is the best response?
options: Correct, the cast is only a problem on ARM
The store is fine but the cast itself is a compile error
In C this is undefined behavior regardless of the CPU; copy with memcpy instead
It is fine as long as buf is a global
explain: The C standard makes a misaligned pointer conversion undefined behavior, so the compiler may emit instructions that assume alignment (for example vector loads that require it). `memcpy` into an `int` is the portable way to read bytes at any address.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: Why is `size_of::<Option<Box<u8>>>()` equal to 8 on a 64-bit target?
options: The compiler stores None in a global table
Option is always pointer-sized
Box is never null, so null encodes None and no tag byte is needed
u8 has alignment 1, so the tag fits inside it
explain: Box<U> is in the std::option list of types where Option<T> has the same size as T. Option is not always pointer-sized: Option<u64> is 16 bytes.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
question: A squat-depth checker flags every rep as too shallow, but only for users who film from directly in front. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OKS sigma for knees is too large
Foreshortening: in a frontal 2D view the thigh points at the camera, so the 2D knee angle looks straighter than it is
The heatmap resolution is too low
Hysteresis thresholds are too far apart
explain: A 2D angle measures the projection. When thigh or shin points toward the camera, it shrinks in the image and the projected angle opens up (111 degrees in 3D looked like 173 in the example). OKS sigmas only affect evaluation.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
question: An Elasticsearch shard holds a single segment, k = 10 and default num_candidates. The kNN filter matches 12 documents in that segment. What does Lucene do?
options: Walks the HNSW graph and returns at most 10 of the 12
Skips the graph and scores the 12 matching documents directly
Runs the unfiltered search, then applies the filter as a post-filter
Raises an error because matches are fewer than num_candidates
explain: Default num_candidates is 1.5 x 10 = 15. Since 12 matches is no more than 15, Lucene's documented rule skips the graph and brute-forces the 12 filtered documents for that segment.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
question: A loop does about 30 cycles of work per iteration and each miss costs about 250 cycles. Using the simple model, what is the smallest prefetch distance that hides the miss?
explain: $d \ge \lceil 250 / 30 \rceil = \lceil 8.33 \rceil = 9$. With d = 8 the prefetch is issued only 240 cycles ahead, 10 cycles short, so the miss is not fully hidden: the model gives $\max(30, 250/8) = 31.25$ cycles per iteration instead of 30.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: A step is mathematically correct, but its soft-estimation label is 0.125 (1 of 8 rollouts succeeded). What is the best explanation?
options: The step is subtly wrong; SE is never low for correct steps
Soft labels are always one eighth of hard labels
The completer rarely finishes this hard problem correctly, so SE measures the policy's success chance, not step correctness
The reference answer must be wrong
explain: SE is a Monte Carlo value estimate for the completer's policy. On a hard problem even correct prefixes rarely finish well. This is the PRM-versus-value-model confusion the Qwen team identified.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
question: A 16 GiB database process calls `fork()` to take a snapshot, and the child only reads memory and writes it to disk while the parent keeps serving writes. Which cost grows over time?
options: None: copy-on-write means fork never copies data
The child's reads, because reading a shared page triggers a copy
The parent's writes: each first write to a still-shared page faults and copies that page, so memory use grows with the number of distinct pages the parent modifies
The initial fork, which copies all 16 GiB before returning
explain: Reads of shared pages are free. Each page the parent modifies while the child still maps it must be copied once, so both memory use and page-fault work grow with the parent's write set during the snapshot.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
question: You use m = 16 sub-quantizers with k* = 256 on 512-dim float32 vectors. How many bytes does each PQ code take, and what is the compression ratio?
options: 16 bytes, 128x smaller than 2,048 bytes
256 bytes, 8x smaller
64 bytes, because each sub-vector stores 32 dims
2 bytes, because 16 codes x 1 bit
explain: Each of the 16 indices takes log2(256) = 8 bits = 1 byte, so 16 bytes. The raw vector is 512 x 4 = 2,048 bytes, so the ratio is 128x. The sub-vector width (32 dims) changes the codebook size, not the code size.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
question: Your team tuned a prompt by hand to 91% on model X. Leadership switches to model Y. What does the evidence in this lesson suggest?
options: The prompt will keep roughly its 91% because its meaning has not changed
Re-run the search on model Y with the same metric and dev set, because the best prompt and format are model-specific
Add "You are an expert" to the prompt, since personas transfer across models
Only the few-shot examples need changing, never the instruction
explain: Sclar et al. found format performance only weakly correlates between models, and on GSM8K the APE trigger beat "Let's think step by step." with InstructGPT (43.0% versus 40.7%) but lost with PaLM 2-L (58.8% versus 71.8%). Keep the metric and data, and re-optimize for the new model.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
question: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock's simple prompt optimization matches the AWS docs?
options: It searches over many candidates and returns the one with the best score on your data
It performs a fast heuristic rewrite of one prompt for one chosen model and does not use evaluation data
It fine-tunes the target model on your prompt
It guarantees the rewritten prompt scores higher on your task
explain: The docs describe simple optimization as a heuristic rewrite of a single short prompt for one model, with no evaluation data and no multi-model support. Evaluation-driven optimization is the separate Advanced Prompt Optimization feature.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: At the start of sampling, what is the distribution of a residue's orientation?
options: The orientation of the nearest residue in the training set
