Close to uniform on SO(3): all orientations equally likely, mean pairwise angle about 126.5 degrees
Identity, because the noise schedule starts from the identity rotation
A Maxwell density with scale 0.45 radians
explain: The large-t limit of IGSO(3) is the uniform (Haar) measure on SO(3). The computed mean angle at t = 4.0 is 124.5 degrees, already within 2 degrees of the uniform limit of 126.5, and the L1 distance between the two densities is 0.045.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
question: Your merchandising team edits the synonym list every week and it includes rules like `tv, television, flat screen`. Which setup fits?
options: synonym filter in the index analyzer, reindex weekly
synonym filter at both index and search time so scores stay consistent
Expand synonyms in application code by duplicating every document
synonym_graph in the search analyzer, backed by a synonym set or an updateable file
explain: Search time lets the list change without reindexing, and synonym_graph is the filter that handles the multi-word entry flat screen correctly. The index-time synonym filter cannot store multi-position tokens faithfully.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
question: Your chat RAG app concatenates the last five turns into the retrieval query. Users report that after they switch topic, answers keep citing documents about the old topic. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the number of retrieved passages so the new topic also appears
Rewrite the latest turn into a standalone query using the history, and retrieve with that alone
Concatenate only the last two turns instead of five
Embed each turn separately and average the vectors
explain: Concatenation (with any window) and averaging both keep old-topic words in the query. A rewriter reads the history to resolve references but outputs only what the current turn needs, so a topic switch produces a query about the new topic.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
question: With the default model (TTFT 0.3 s, 100 tokens/s), you can either run 3 independent sub-queries generated by one call, or a 3-hop Self-Ask chain. Why is the chain slower?
options: The chain retrieves more documents
Each hop needs the previous hop's answer, so its LLM calls (each paying TTFT) run one after another instead of being merged into one call
Self-Ask uses a larger model by definition
Parallel queries skip the reader
explain: Independent sub-queries come out of a single generation call and are searched in parallel, so the critical path has one extra call. A chain has one call per hop on the critical path, and every call pays TTFT plus decoding again.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
question: A colleague estimates inner products with <o-bar,q> directly, skipping the division. What happens to a ranking of documents for one query?
options: Nothing; the ranking is identical because every estimate is scaled by exactly the same constant
Estimates become unbiased but noisier
Each document's estimate is scaled by its own <o-bar,o>, which varies per vector, so the ranking gets extra noise and the distances are biased
The code must be recomputed
explain: The scaling factor is not a global constant: it is about 0.8 on average but differs from vector to vector, because it depends on how evenly each rotated vector spreads its length. The paper also notes this direct estimator is provably biased, which matters when plugged into equation (2) for distances.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
question: Server S2 is a follower with currentTerm 4. It receives RequestVote from S4 for term 3. What does S2 do?
options: Grants the vote if it has not voted yet in term 3
Rejects it and replies with term 4, so S4 learns it is behind
Becomes a candidate for term 5
Adopts term 3 and grants the vote
explain: Any request with a stale term is rejected, and the reply carries the responder's current term. When S4 sees term 4 it updates its term and returns to follower. Terms never go backward.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
question: A team fine-tunes an LLM on their product docs every quarter. Docs change weekly, and users need links to the source page. What does RAG give them that fine-tuning does not?
options: Higher fluency, because retrieved text improves the model's grammar
Fresh facts by re-indexing without retraining, and provenance because the answer can cite the retrieved chunk
Lower latency, because retrieval is always faster than generation
Nothing; fine-tuning and RAG update knowledge in the same way
explain: The index is non-parametric memory: changing it changes what the model can see, as the hot-swap experiment showed (68% vs 4% on 2018 leaders, with the 2018 vs the 2016 index). And because the evidence is an explicit chunk, the answer can point to it. Retrieval adds a step, so it does not lower latency.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
question: Your RAG chatbot gives wrong answers on 20% of test questions. On those, context recall averages 0.95 and faithfulness 0.55. Where should you work first?
options: The chunker: chunks are too small
Top-k: retrieve more chunks
The generation side: the right facts are in context but the answers make unsupported claims
The embedding model: retrieval is missing facts
explain: Context recall near 1 says the evidence is reaching the prompt. Faithfulness of 0.55 says nearly half the statements are not supported by it. That points at the prompt, the context noise, or the model, not at retrieval.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
question: You compute title BM25 for one document using IDF from the body field because it is already cached. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, IDF is a property of the term
Terms that are common in bodies but rare in titles get far too little weight in the title feature
The score becomes negative
Coverage stops working
explain: IDF depends on the field's own document frequencies. In the toy, fast has IDF 0.875 in titles but 0.087 in bodies. Using body IDF would make a title match on fast look almost worthless.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
question: A query has R = 3 relevant documents and your system ranks all 3 at the top. What is its P@10?
options: 1.0, since the ranking is perfect
0.3, since P@10 is capped at R/k
0.1, since only the first one counts
Undefined, since R is less than k
explain: P@10 divides hits by 10 no matter how many relevant documents exist, so 3/10 = 0.3 is the best possible. This is why P@k averaged over queries partly measures how many relevant documents each query has. R-precision (P@3 here) would give 1.0.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Implementation gotchas: ties, ideals, missing queries
question: Your new dense retriever scores 0.20 nDCG@10 lower than BM25 on an old TREC collection, and Judged@10 for it is 0.55 (BM25: 0.95). What should you conclude?
options: The dense retriever is clearly worse
Switch to exponential gain to fix the gap
Use MRR instead, which ignores unjudged documents
Nothing reliable yet: 45% of its top 10 is unjudged and counted as nonrelevant, so its score is a lower bound; judge those documents or report with judged_only
explain: Old qrels were pooled from old systems. Unjudged documents count as nonrelevant, which systematically penalizes a system that retrieves different documents. Low Judged@k is a warning that the comparison is biased, not evidence that the system is bad. MRR treats unjudged documents the same way.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A peer's RDMA WRITE targets `remote_addr = 0x15040` in the 8-page region starting at `0x10000` (4 KB pages). Which page index and byte offset does the NIC write?
options: Page 4, offset 0x40
Page 5, offset 0x400
Page 5, offset 64
Page 21, offset 64
explain: Offset = 0x15040 - 0x10000 = 0x5040 = 20544 bytes. 20544 / 4096 = 5 remainder 64. So page index 5 at byte 64 (0x40). Page 21 comes from forgetting to subtract the base.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: A 64-node cluster with 24 threads per node uses one RC QP between every pair of threads. Using FaRM's formula, how many QPs does each machine hold, and what is the likely symptom?
options: 2 x 64 x 24 = 3072; none, QPs are free
64 x 24 = 1536; the CQ overflows
24 x 24 = 576; RNR errors
2 x 64 x 24 x 24 = 73,728; throughput drops from QP-state cache misses on the NIC
explain: 2mt squared = 2 x 64 x 576 = 73,728. QP state lives in host memory with the NIC caching it; FaRM saw request rates fall as the cluster grew for exactly this reason. One QP per thread per machine (3072) or sharing among q threads cuts it.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
question: A racing game with heavy, fast cars shows remote cars stuttering. Which technique fits best before adding interpolation delay?
options: Dead reckoning from last known speed and heading, corrected by each update
Lag compensation
Server reconciliation of remote cars
Masking WebSocket frames
explain: A fast car cannot change direction instantly, so its position is predictable from speed and heading: the classic case for dead reckoning. Lag compensation is about hit tests; reconciliation applies to your own inputs.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Matrix factorization: learning user and item vectors
question: You have billions of implicit events (every user-item pair counts) and a cluster of machines. Which optimizer do Koren et al. suggest, and why?
options: SGD, because it is always faster than ALS
Neither; matrix factorization cannot use implicit data
SGD with a larger learning rate, to make up for the dense data
ALS, because each user (and each item) vector is an independent least-squares solve that parallelizes, and it avoids looping over every cell of a dense matrix
explain: Both reasons are stated in the paper: ALS parallelizes naturally, and for implicit data the training set is not sparse, so per-cell SGD loops are impractical. Hu et al. show how ALS stays linear in the number of non-zeros.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
question: Your new model beats matrix factorization on a random 80/20 holdout of watch events. Before shipping, what is the most important check?
options: Re-run with a different random seed for the same 80/20 split
Evaluate with a temporal split (train on the past, predict later events) against tuned baselines, then A/B test
Switch the metric from recall@k to RMSE
Add more epochs until offline recall stops improving
explain: A random holdout lets the model see a user's future and future popularity. A temporal split matches deployment, tuned simple baselines guard against weak comparisons (Dacrema et al.), and only an online test measures the real effect.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
question: The outer side of a join yields 10 rows after a filter. The inner table has 10000 rows and a B-tree index on the join key. Which plan is most likely cheapest?
options: Nested loop with an index scan on the inner side
Hash join, building on the 10000-row table
Merge join after sorting both sides
Nested loop with a sequential scan of the inner side
explain: Ten index lookups touch only a few pages each, while a hash join must read all 10000 inner rows once. The PostgreSQL docs show exactly this case (unique1 < 10) choosing Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan. A nested loop with a sequential inner scan would read the 10000-row table 10 times.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
question: A web app writes a profile update to the primary, then immediately reads it from a synchronous standby configured with `synchronous_commit = on`. Users sometimes see the old profile. Why?
options: The standby is asynchronous despite the setting
Synchronous replication only applies to DDL statements
The standby flushed the WAL record but had not yet replayed it when the read arrived
The primary acknowledged before flushing its own WAL
explain: `on` waits for the standby to flush the commit record to disk, not to apply it. Replay is a separate step, so a read can arrive in between. `remote_apply` closes that gap at a higher commit latency, or the app can read its own writes from the primary.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
question: Vector clocks: version X = [(Sx,3),(Sy,1)] and version Y = [(Sx,2),(Sy,2)]. What should a Dynamo-style store do on a read that finds both?
options: Return both as concurrent siblings
Keep X, since Sx's counter is larger
Keep Y, since it has the larger total
Keep whichever has the later wall-clock timestamp
explain: X is ahead on Sx (3 vs 2) but behind on Sy (1 vs 2), so neither descends from the other. They are concurrent, and the store returns both for reconciliation. Picking by one counter, a sum or a wall clock would silently drop an update.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
question: You run GRPO on coding tasks with reward = 1 if pytest exits successfully. Which change most directly closes the hacks in this lesson?
options: Lower the learning rate so hacks are learned more slowly
Run the grader outside the agent's sandbox on fresh copies of the tests, check results per test instead of the exit status, and remove reference solutions from the environment
Increase the group size from 4 to 16
Add a format reward for well-commented code
explain: Each hack exploits something the agent can touch: the exit status, the test files, pytest internals, or leftover answers. Isolating the grader removes those levers. A lower learning rate or bigger group changes how fast or how noisily the hack spreads, not whether it pays.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
question: A team runs disaggregated pools with strict on-policy synchronous training and sees each pool idle about half the time. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Switch to FP8 weights for the rollout engine
Increase the KV cache size
Either colocate the pools or let rollout of the next batch overlap training on the current one with bounded staleness
Add more training GPUs
explain: Strict alternation between two separate pools means each pool waits for the other. Colocation lets one pool do both phases; overlap keeps both pools busy at the cost of one or more steps of staleness. The other changes speed up one phase but keep the alternation.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
question: Your Triad kernel a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i] on 2^25 doubles takes 0.30 ms. What effective bandwidth do you report?
options: 1,789.6 GB/s, counting only the two arrays read
894.8 GB/s, counting one array
2,684.4 GB/s, counting two reads and one write
3,579.1 GB/s, counting four arrays
explain: Triad reads b and c and writes a: three arrays of 268.4 MB, 805.3 MB total. 805.3 MB / 0.30 ms = 2,684.4 GB/s. BabelStream gives Triad a weight of 3 for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: What touched it last: change correlation and bisection
question: You can bisect 128 deploys in 7 tests, each costing one minute of degraded traffic on 1 percent of users. Your incident is a full outage. What is the right order of operations?
options: Bisect immediately: finding the cause is the fastest route to recovery
Bisect, but skip the tests that would affect users
Roll back all 128 deploys at once, then bisect to find the cause at leisure if the rollback worked
Mitigate first (roll back to the last known good state or shed the broken path), then bisect afterwards with no user impact
explain: During a full outage, 7 minutes spent bisecting is 7 minutes of outage, and the troubleshooting chapter is explicit that stopping the bleeding comes first. Rolling everything back is a legitimate mitigation, but on its own it omits the ordering that matters: mitigate, then investigate on a canary while users are served.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: RRF next to CombSUM, CombMNZ, Borda and Condorcet
question: Which of these methods needs each system's scores, not just its ranks?
options: CombMNZ
Borda count
Condorcet fusion
RRF
explain: CombSUM and CombMNZ add similarity values (Fox and Shaw combined similarities, typically normalized). Borda, Condorcet and RRF use only the order of each list, which is why they work when scores are missing or incomparable.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
question: Why does the kernel make `Guard` impossible to send to another thread?
options: Moving the guard would copy the protected data and break the lock
A kernel mutex must be unlocked by the task that locked it, and the guard's drop is that unlock
Guards are allocated on the stack, and stacks cannot be shared
Sending would require the data `T` to be `Copy`
explain: Dropping a Guard calls `mutex_unlock()`. If the guard could cross to another thread, the unlock would run there, violating the C rule that only the owner may unlock. The `NotThreadSafe` marker makes the compiler reject that.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Why the kernel lets a BPF program pick the next thread
question: Which problem does sched_ext mainly remove compared with patching CFS directly?
options: Scheduling decisions must be made in user space, which adds a context switch per pick
BPF programs run faster than compiled kernel C, so a fixed policy becomes cheaper
Each policy change needs a kernel rebuild, reboot, workload rewarm and fleet rollout, and a bug can crash the host
The fair class cannot run on machines with more than one L3 cache
explain: The motivation is iteration speed and safety: a policy is loaded and unloaded like a program, and the kernel can always revert to fair. BPF schedulers mostly run in the kernel (user space involvement is optional), and BPF is not faster than native kernel code.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
question: A scheduler with the default timeout has a bug: tasks of one cgroup are inserted into a custom DSQ that dispatch never reads. What do you observe?
options: Those tasks freeze, then within about 30 to 45 s the scheduler is unloaded with a stall error and everything runs on fair again
The machine hangs until rebooted because BPF code runs with interrupts disabled
The verifier refuses to load the scheduler because a DSQ is never consumed
The tasks run anyway because custom DSQs fall back to the global DSQ after one slice
explain: The verifier checks memory safety and termination, not whether your policy eventually runs every task. The watchdog sees runnable tasks older than 30 s on its next check (every 15 s), exits with SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL, and tasks revert to the fair class.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
question: Why can Self-Rewarding training, at least in principle, raise its own ceiling, while SPIN cannot exceed its SFT data?
options: Self-Rewarding uses DPO and SPIN does not
Self-Rewarding trains on more prompts
In Self-Rewarding the judge is the model being trained, so its preferences can improve each iteration; SPIN always treats the fixed human response as the winner
SPIN uses a smaller base model
explain: Both losses are DPO-like. The difference is the target: SPIN's chosen response is always from the fixed human data, so p_data is the fixed point. Self-Rewarding's preferences come from a judge that is retrained every iteration, which is also why it carries a risk of reward hacking that SPIN does not.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: Which of the two can return an answer that is wrong for the current question even though the model would have answered correctly?
options: Provider prompt caching
Neither, since both check the full prompt
Semantic caching
Both equally
explain: Prompt caching only skips recomputing an identical prefix; the answer is still generated for the full current prompt. A semantic cache returns an answer generated for a different prompt, and a false hit is exactly that failure.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Compressed FSMs: decoding several tokens in one step
question: Which constraint gives jump-forward decoding the largest saving?
options: A free-text field `[\w\s]{1,500}` with no other structure
A schema with long constant key names and enums whose options differ in their first character
A regex that accepts any digit sequence
Plain decoding with no constraint at all
explain: Savings come from compressed edges: text the grammar fully determines. Long keys and early-diverging enums create long forced runs. Free text and open digit runs leave a real choice at every token, so nothing can be skipped.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
question: Suppose one arc had weight -5 (say, a modeled time bonus). What breaks?
options: Correctness: a settled node's label might later be beaten through the negative arc
Only performance: the answer stays correct but slower
Nothing, as long as there is no negative cycle
The priority queue cannot store negative keys
explain: The finality argument assumes the rest of any path adds nonnegative length. A negative arc can make a path through a far node cheaper than an already settled label. Label-correcting methods such as Bellman-Ford handle negative weights, at higher cost.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Sampling: why a 7 Hz wave sampled at 10 Hz looks like 3 Hz
question: You have 1000 Hz sensor data and want 100 Hz. A colleague writes `y = x[::10]`. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: keeping every 10th sample is exactly what downsampling means
Content between 50 and 500 Hz folds into the 0 to 50 Hz band, because nothing removed it first
The result has the wrong length; it should be `x[::100]`
Slicing shifts the phase by half a sample, which is the only error
explain: Keeping every 10th sample makes the new Nyquist frequency 50 Hz. Anything in the original data between 50 and 500 Hz now aliases into 0 to 50 Hz. Low-pass filter first, or use `scipy.signal.decimate(x, 10)`, which filters then downsamples.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
question: How many 8-bit integers does one AVX-512 `zmm` register hold, and how many 64-bit doubles?
options: 64 and 8
16 and 2
32 and 4
explain: 512 bits / 8 bits = 64 bytes, and 512 / 64 = 8 doubles. 512 and 64 would be counting bits, not lanes; 16 and 2 is the 128-bit case.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
question: The same SVE saxpy binary runs with n = 10 on a 128-bit and a 512-bit implementation. How many loop iterations does each run?
options: 3 and 1
10 and 10
3 and 3, because the binary was compiled for 128 bits
2 and 1
explain: With 4 lanes the loop runs at i = 0, 4, 8 (the last with T T F F). With 16 lanes one iteration covers all 10 elements under a 10-true predicate. The lane count is read at run time by incw and svcntw.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
question: A bump pointer sits at offset 13 in a chunk. The next request is 16 bytes with alignment 8. At which offset does the object start, and where does the pointer end up (bumping upwards)?
options: Starts at 13, pointer ends at 29
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 32
Starts at 8, pointer ends at 24
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 29
explain: Round 13 up to a multiple of 8: (13 + 7) & ~7 = 16. Then add the size: 16 + 16 = 32. The 3 bytes at offsets 13 to 15 are padding.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
question: You have a fixed 64-GPU budget for a math RLVR run with a synchronous loop and short, similar-length responses. Which placement fits the GLM-4.5 report's guidance?
options: 32 rollout GPUs and 32 training GPUs in separate pools, synchronous
Colocated with --colocate, so all 64 GPUs alternate between rollout and training
Separate pools with fully async rollout and maximal staleness
Rollout-only, with training on CPU
explain: For reasoning tasks the report uses colocated synchronous training with dynamic sampling. A synchronous loop on split pools leaves each half idle while the other works.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Launching and debugging a slime run
question: Generations look like garbage, and you suspect either the FP8 rollout checkpoint or the weight sync. Which first step isolates the inference side cheaply?
options: Run with `--debug-train-only`
Run with `--debug-rollout-only` on a few GPUs to see whether SGLang alone generates coherent text from the checkpoint
Increase `--global-batch-size`
Disable `--colocate`
explain: The debug guide suggests `--debug-rollout-only` with few GPUs to test the quantized checkpoint alone; if it is fine, look at the sync with `--check-weight-update-equal`.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
question: The ordinary kriging system has an extra row of ones and an extra unknown $\mu$. What would go wrong if you dropped them and just solved $\Gamma \boldsymbol\lambda = \boldsymbol\gamma_0$?
options: The weights would no longer be forced to sum to 1, so the estimate would be biased whenever the unknown mean is not zero
Nothing; the row only speeds up the solve
The estimate would ignore the nearest sensor
The matrix would become 8 by 8
explain: The constraint row enforces $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$, which makes the estimate unbiased for any constant mean. Without it the weights can sum to anything, and the estimate is pulled toward or away from zero.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: Why does the target pass produce gamma + 1 distributions rather than gamma?
options: Causal attention gives a next-token distribution after every input token, including after the last guess, which supplies a bonus token when all guesses pass
One extra position is needed to check the prefix
The draft also returns one distribution that is reused
It is an implementation detail that is never used
explain: The forward pass over prefix plus gamma guesses outputs a distribution after each of them. The last one, after guess gamma, is a free target prediction used only when all guesses are accepted, raising the maximum to gamma + 1 tokens per round.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: In Whisper-Streaming you raise MinChunkSize, the minimum new audio processed per update. What happens?
options: Latency rises, but each update sees more audio, so quality tends to improve
Latency drops, because fewer updates are needed
Nothing, because LocalAgreement only depends on text
WER rises, because the 30 s window overflows
explain: The paper describes MinChunkSize as the parameter that controls latency and quality. Bigger chunks mean waiting longer before each update, but each transcription has more context. The paper also found the computationally unaware latency (ignoring compute time) to be about twice the chunk size, since two consecutive updates must agree. Buffers are trimmed at sentence ends to stay near 30 s, so overflow is not the issue.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: Why is calling munmap on a small buffer often slower in a 64-thread process than in a single-threaded one?
options: The kernel must shoot down stale TLB entries on every CPU running the process, using IPIs and waiting for them
munmap must zero the pages first
Each thread has its own page table that must be edited
munmap takes a global lock across all processes
explain: Threads share one page table, so any CPU running one of them might cache the translation. The initiating CPU interrupts those CPUs and waits for them to flush before the pages can be reused. Threads do not have separate page tables, and freed pages are not zeroed at munmap.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: erasing refusal from the residual stream
question: You want to stop refusals. Option A subtracts the refusal vector (x minus r) at one layer. Option B ablates r-hat at every layer. Arditi et al. found both bypass refusal comparably. What is B's advantage on harmless prompts?
options: B is faster at inference
B also improves MMLU
A shifts every activation by a fixed amount, pushing harmless ones far past zero; B only removes what is there, so it raised loss on harmless data less
There is no difference on harmless prompts
explain: Subtraction moves all activations by the same vector, so prompts with little refusal content end up strongly negative along r, an unnatural state. Ablation sets the component to zero regardless. In the paper's comparison, activation addition in the negative direction caused higher loss on harmless data than directional ablation.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: Sensors publish at QoS 1. Your rollup job sums energy readings per minute and the totals are occasionally slightly too high. Most likely cause?
options: QoS 1 can lose messages, and losses push sums up
QoS 1 retries after a lost PUBACK, so a reading can be delivered twice and counted twice
Kafka reorders records within a partition
MQTT always runs over UDP, which duplicates packets
explain: At least once means no loss but possible duplicates. A sum counts a duplicate twice. The fix is to deduplicate on a reading id (device id plus sequence number) or to write results idempotently, covered in the last lesson.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Per Table 1 of the paper, for which sequences is one self-attention layer cheaper in total work than one recurrent layer?
options: Always, because it has O(1) sequential operations
When the sequence length n is larger than the model width d
When n is smaller than d, which is typical for sentence-length inputs
Never; it is only faster because of parallelism
explain: Self-attention costs about $n^2 d$ and a recurrent layer about $n d^2$, so attention does less total work when $n < d$. The paper notes this is usually the case for sentences with d = 512. Sequential operations are a separate column: they measure parallelism, not total work.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: You increase the context length of a model from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens and keep d fixed. Roughly how does the score-matrix work per layer change?
options: It grows about 4 times, like the FFN
It grows about 16 times, while the FFN work grows about 4 times
It stays the same because heads run in parallel
It grows about 2 times
explain: Score work scales with n^2: (16384/4096)^2 = 16. The FFN and projections scale with n, so they grow 4 times. Parallel heads change wall-clock time, not the amount of work.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
question: An Elasticsearch index has 5 shards and a rare term that happens to be concentrated in one shard. Why might the same document get a slightly different BM25 score than in a single-shard index?
options: IDF and avgdl are computed from per-shard statistics by default
BM25 uses random tie-breaking
k1 is divided by the number of shards
Norms are only stored on the primary shard
explain: Lucene computes N, n_t and avgdl from the index it searches. In Elasticsearch each shard is a separate Lucene index, and the default query_then_fetch search type scores with local, per-shard term and document frequencies. Skewed terms then get different IDFs per shard. The dfs_query_then_fetch search type gathers global frequencies first, at extra cost.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Training loss is going down very slowly and smoothly, and you know the gradients are correct. Which change most directly speeds things up?
options: Increase the learning rate moderately and watch for oscillation
Flip the sign of the update so you move along the gradient
Decrease the learning rate
Stop training; slow progress means a minimum was reached
explain: Smooth, slow decrease is the signature of a learning rate that is too small (like $\eta = 0.05$ here). Raise it gradually; if the loss starts to oscillate or climb you have passed the stable limit. Moving along the gradient would increase the loss.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
question: `grep -c error app.log > count.txt` prints `grep: app.log: No such file or directory` on the terminal. Why is that message not in count.txt?
options: count.txt is opened only after grep succeeds
grep prints errors through the shell, not through a file descriptor
Error messages go to fd 2, and only fd 1 was redirected
Redirection is ignored when the command fails
explain: The shell opens count.txt on fd 1 before exec, whether or not grep succeeds (so count.txt now exists, empty). grep writes its complaint to fd 2, which still points at the terminal.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: Two words, *Paris* and *Rome*, never appear in the same sentence in the training corpus. Can skip-gram still give them similar vectors?
options: No, they must co-occur to be pulled together
Yes, if they share many context words such as city, capital and visited
Only if they are in the same window at least once
Only with CBOW, not skip-gram
explain: Similarity comes from shared contexts, not direct co-occurrence. Both input vectors are trained to score highly against the same output vectors (u_city, u_capital, ...), which pushes them toward the same region of the space.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: Which statement about running `./hello` is correct?
options: The shell reads hello's machine code and executes it itself
The CPU loads the ELF file from disk one instruction at a time as it runs
The kernel, via execve, replaces the current process image with hello and starts it at its entry point
The linker runs again every time you start the program
explain: execve(2): the program currently run by the calling process is replaced with a new one, with a newly initialized stack, heap and data segments. The CPU never reads from the disk file directly; pages of the file are mapped into memory and loaded when touched.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
The C library has no way to call functions
explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
It is required by the softmax
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It prevents the prompt from being masked
explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 3). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: A function `void clear(char *buf)` does `memset(buf, 0, sizeof buf);` and callers pass a `char buf[256]`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, sizeof buf is 256
It clears only 8 bytes, because buf is a pointer inside the function
It clears 257 bytes including the terminator
It fails to compile because arrays cannot be passed
explain: Inside clear, buf is a char *, so sizeof buf is the pointer size (8 on 64-bit platforms), not 256. The array's size is lost at the call. The fix is `void clear(char *buf, size_t n)` and `memset(buf, 0, n)`.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
options: None; `drop` is special and can be called twice
`drop(s)`, because the first iteration moves `s` into `drop` and the second iteration uses a moved value
`for _ in 0..2`, because loops cannot capture Strings
explain: `drop` is an ordinary function taking its argument by value, so the first call moves `s`. The compiler sees the loop can run again and reports E0382 (use of moved value). This is a double free the compiler caught.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
question: A tree where each child needs a pointer back to its parent, and nodes are created and removed while the program runs. Which choice fits best?
options: Plain `&Node` references stored in each child
`Rc` from parent to children and `Weak` from child to parent (with `RefCell` where nodes must change)
Clone the parent into each child
explain: Nodes have no single owner whose scope covers every use, which is what plain references need. Cloning would give each child a separate copy rather than the real parent. `Rc` counts owners; a `Weak` back-pointer does not count, so parent and child do not keep each other alive in a cycle that leaks. `RefCell` allows mutation, checked at run time. This is the Book's tree design.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
question: You need $ABx$ where $A$ and $B$ are $1000 \times 1000$ and $x$ is a vector. Which order of evaluation is cheaper?
options: (AB)x, because multiplying matrices first is faster
A(Bx), because two matrix-vector products cost about 2 million multiply-adds versus about 1 billion for AB
They cost the same because multiplication is associative
Neither; you must invert A first
explain: Associativity guarantees the same answer, not the same cost. $AB$ alone is $1000^3 = 10^9$ multiply-adds. $B\mathbf{x}$ then $A(B\mathbf{x})$ is $2 \times 1000^2 = 2\times10^6$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
question: You can't change the degree-9 model. Which change most directly reduces its overfitting?
options: Train longer to reach exactly zero training loss
Collect more training data from the same distribution
Evaluate on the training set instead
Increase the learning rate
explain: More data constrains the same model: median test RMS fell from 0.643 at N = 10 to 0.340 at N = 100. Training longer only drives it further into the noise, and evaluating on training data hides the problem.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
question: Why is backpropagation so much cheaper than finite differences for a network with N weights?
options: It uses lower precision arithmetic
It only computes gradients for the last layer
It skips the forward pass
It reuses each node's upstream gradient for all of that node's inputs, so one backward pass of similar cost to the forward pass gives all N derivatives
explain: Finite differences need about N+1 forward passes because each one measures a single derivative. Backprop shares the work: a gradient computed once at a node is reused by everything upstream of it, so the full gradient costs a small constant times one forward pass.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
question: Using the same 64-byte address space and page table (VP 0 to frame 3, VP 1 to 7, VP 2 to 5, VP 3 to 2), what physical address does virtual address 40 map to?
explain: 40 is 101000 in binary: VPN 10 = 2 and offset 1000 = 8. VP 2 lives in frame 5, so the physical address is 5 x 16 + 8 = 88. Answer 40 forgets translation; 72 would be frame 4; 117 is the earlier example.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
question: A fraud model flags 95% of fraudulent transactions and 2% of legitimate ones. Fraud is 0.1% of transactions. Roughly what fraction of flagged transactions are fraud?
options: About 95%
About 50%
About 4.5%
About 0.1%
explain: Per 100,000 transactions: 100 fraud, 95 flagged; 99,900 legitimate, 1,998 flagged. 95 / (95 + 1,998) = 0.045. The flagging rate on fraud (95%) is recall, not precision; the tiny base rate makes most flags false alarms.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
question: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for a lift in click rate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new variant is not better
There is a 97% chance the lift is real
If there were no true difference, a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time
The lift is large enough to matter for the business
explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true: it is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data). Getting the probability that the variant is better needs a prior and Bayes' rule. And p says nothing about whether the effect size matters.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: GPT-3 used about 3.2e+23 FLOPs. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter, what would a compute-optimal model at that budget look like?
options: 175B parameters on 300B tokens
About 500B parameters on 105B tokens
About 12B parameters on 4.3T tokens
About 51B parameters on 1.0T tokens
explain: Set $D = 20N$, so $C = 6 \cdot N \cdot 20N = 120N^2$ and $N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 51$B, $D \approx 1.0$T. GPT-3's actual 175B on 300B tokens is the Kaplan-style choice; 12B on 4.3T overshoots the token ratio badly.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size
question: You will store 10 million passages as 384-dimensional float32 vectors. Roughly how much memory do the raw vectors need?
options: 1.5 GB
3.8 GB
explain: 10,000,000 x 384 x 4 bytes = 15,360,000,000 bytes, about 15.4 GB, before any index overhead such as HNSW graph links. 3.8 GB would be 1 byte per dimension; 30.7 GB would be 768 dimensions.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
question: Encode newer with the 10 toy merges. What comes out?
options: new e r _
new er_
n e w e r _
ne w e r _
explain: Pairs present at the start: (n,e) rank 6, (e,w) and others unranked. Merge (n,e), then (ne,w) rank 7 gives new. Remaining pairs (new,e), (e,r), (r,_) are not in the list, so the result is new e r _. No er_ token was learned.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
question: You switch from `torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)` to `torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)`. What changes?
options: Nothing; the two classes are aliases
Decay is now applied directly as w -= lr x 0.01 x w, instead of being added to the gradient and rescaled by 1/sqrt(v)
AdamW disables bias correction
AdamW applies decay only to biases
explain: Adam's weight_decay adds lambda x w to the gradient, which then passes through the m/sqrt(v) ratio. AdamW shrinks the weights in a separate step, so every weight decays at the rate lr x lambda regardless of its gradient history.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
question: An index returns 10 results for a query; 7 of them are among the true 10 nearest neighbors. A colleague says recall@10 is 0.7, but because the 7 are ranked in a different order than the exact ones, the real recall is lower. Who is right?
options: The colleague: order mismatches reduce recall@10
Neither: recall needs the distances, not the ids
You: recall@10 counts overlap with the true top 10, so it is 0.7
The colleague: recall@10 is only defined for exact order
explain: Recall@k, as defined in the HNSW paper, is the number of true nearest neighbors found divided by k. It is a set overlap; ranking quality inside the top k is a separate metric.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events
question: A token's fitted probability hits exactly 0 at generation 4 of this fully synthetic loop. What is the chance it reappears at generation 50?
options: About its original probability, because errors average out over generations
Small but positive, because sampling is random
Zero, because a token with probability 0 is never sampled and refitting cannot invent it
About 1/M, because each generation draws M fresh samples
explain: The histogram model can only assign mass to tokens it has seen. Once a count is zero the token has probability zero, so no later sample contains it. Only an outside source of real data could bring it back.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: Which change most directly addresses the failure that phi-1's authors warned about when prompting a model to write textbooks?
options: Lower the sampling temperature for cleaner text
Generate ten times more textbooks from the same prompt
Vary the topic and target audience in each generation prompt
Train the student for more epochs on the synthetic set
explain: Their concern was homogeneous, redundant output: a generator repeats its most probable content. Constraining topics and audiences forces coverage. Lower temperature and more samples from one prompt make redundancy worse.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
question: You are building a key-value store for datasets 10 times larger than RAM on fast NVMe drives, with transactional writes. Which design does the CIDR 2022 evidence favor?
options: mmap the whole file with MAP_SHARED and rely on msync at commit
A user-space buffer pool with explicit reads and writes (for example pread or io_uring)
mmap with MADV_RANDOM, since it matched fio in the paper
mmap with MAP_POPULATE so all pages are resident up front
explain: MADV_RANDOM matched fio only until the page cache filled; then eviction overhead cut throughput to about half. MAP_SHARED also lets the OS write uncommitted pages at any time. MAP_POPULATE cannot make 10x RAM resident. A buffer pool controls eviction, write ordering and error handling.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: Hedging after the p95 expected latency costs about 5% extra load. Why not hedge immediately (send to two replicas at time 0) to cut the tail further?
options: It would double the load, raising queueing and utilization so much that latency for everyone can get worse
It is forbidden by TCP
It would not reduce latency at all
Replicas cannot answer the same request twice
explain: Sending every request twice doubles the work. Higher utilization lengthens queues, a main source of tail latency. Waiting for a high-percentile delay hedges only the requests likely to be stuck, giving most of the benefit for a few percent extra load; tied requests with cancellation are another way to keep the overhead small.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: Which pair of toy roles is in the relation *finishes*?
options: B finishes A
C finishes D
E finishes D
A finishes C
explain: E (Mar 2024 to Present) and D (Sep 2021 to Present) end at the same point and E starts later, so E finishes D. B is during A, A is before C, and C overlaps or precedes D depending on the convention.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: Beam search with a PRM beats best-of-N at 16 generations but loses at 256 on easy questions. What is the best explanation?
options: Beam search runs out of beams at large N
With more budget the search finds candidates that score high because of PRM errors, not because they are correct
Best-of-N uses a better reward model
Easy questions need more steps than beam search allows
explain: This is verifier over-optimization. Snell et al. saw search produce repetitive or overly short solutions that the PRM still scored well. On easy questions best-of-N's weaker optimization pressure is safer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: During inference with a TTT model, what changes as the model reads a long prompt?
options: Nothing; all weights are frozen at inference
Only the inner weights W inside each TTT layer, which act as a per-sequence hidden state
All model parameters, via backpropagation of next-token loss on the prompt
The projections theta_K, theta_V and theta_Q, which adapt to the prompt
explain: The inner loop runs at inference, so each layer's W takes gradient steps on its self-supervised loss. The outer parameters (projections, W_0, the rest of the network) are learned in training and frozen. No next-token loss is backpropagated at inference.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs
question: In Titans (MAC) at test time, which part keeps changing its weights as the input streams in?
options: The persistent memory tokens
The attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V
All three, since Titans fine-tunes itself at test time
The neural long-term memory M
explain: The paper is explicit: persistent memory parameters stay fixed because they encode task knowledge, the attention weights are fixed in-context learners, and only the long-term memory keeps learning (memorizing) at test time.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
question: Over the last interval a cache's depot held between 120 and 128 full magazines. Using the paper's working-set rule, how many could be reclaimed if memory runs low?
options: 0, magazines are never reclaimed
explain: The working set is the variation, 128 minus 120 = 8 magazines. The 120 magazines that were never touched during the interval are eligible for reclaiming, just as in the paper's 37 to 47 example where 37 are reclaimable.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Demotion: reclaim that migrates instead of swapping
question: Why does TPP keep reclaiming past the normal high watermark on the fast node?
options: To reduce the number of pages on the CXL node
Because reclaim is cheaper when done in larger batches
To make room for short-lived hot allocations and incoming promotions so they land in DRAM instead of spilling to CXL
To keep the inactive list empty
explain: New allocations go to CXL only when the local node is short of free pages. Headroom keeps those bursts local, and promotions need free local frames too. Upstream implements this with the promo watermark.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins
question: Sales of a niche product are 0 in some weeks. A dashboard compares models by MAPE. What goes wrong, and what is a better choice?
options: Nothing, MAPE handles zeros by skipping them
MAPE becomes negative, so use sMAPE instead
MAPE overweights large values, so use RMSE on percentages
MAPE is undefined when actuals are 0 and explodes near 0, so use a scaled metric such as MASE
explain: Percentage errors divide by $y_t$, so a zero actual makes the error infinite or undefined and small actuals dominate the average. MASE divides by the in-sample naive or seasonal naive MAE instead, which is nonzero unless the training series is constant (or, for the seasonal scale, repeats exactly every season). sMAPE is not recommended either.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
question: Why does the fused softmax kernel move about 4x fewer bytes than the five-op PyTorch version?
options: Triton compresses data before writing it to DRAM
Intermediates (max, shifted values, exponentials, sums) stay in registers instead of round-tripping through DRAM
Triton uses fp16 automatically
The fused kernel skips the max subtraction
explain: Each separate op reads its input from DRAM and writes its output back. Fusing keeps all intermediates on chip, leaving one read and one write of the matrix: 2MN instead of 8MN + 4M elements.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
question: A product team wants a Chameleon-style model to read dense receipts and screenshots. What is the main risk the Chameleon paper itself points to?
options: Next-token prediction cannot model 2D layouts at all
The model cannot attend from text to image tokens
The vocabulary has no room for more image codes
The discrete tokenizer reconstructs text-heavy images poorly, which upper-bounds OCR quality
explain: With 13 bits per token and 1024 tokens per 512 px image, fine glyph detail is the first thing lost. The paper calls this a core weakness that bounds OCR-heavy tasks. Separate understanding encoders (lesson 5) are one answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
question: Why did library operating systems from the 1990s, such as Exokernel, never see wide deployment, while unikernels can run on public clouds?
options: Their libraries were written in unsafe languages
They had to support many kinds of real hardware; a hypervisor exposes a few standard virtual devices instead
They required multicore CPUs that did not exist yet
Hypervisors run library OSes faster than bare metal does
explain: The Mirage paper's argument: libOSes struggled with real-world hardware support. A hypervisor's virtual devices (netfront, blkfront, virtio) are a small, stable target, so only a few simple drivers are needed.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: Which service is the weakest candidate for a unikernel?
options: A stateless HTTP API that must cold-start in milliseconds per request burst
A DNS server facing the internet where attack surface matters
A UDP packet processor that needs millions of packets per second per core
A CI build runner that shells out to compilers, git and test scripts in many child processes
explain: The build runner depends on fork, exec and many separate programs, which a single-process, single-address-space unikernel does not support. The other three match unikernel strengths: fast boot, small attack surface and low-level I/O specialization.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
question: Your 768-d fp32 index needs 31 GB and the machine has 16 GB for page cache. Which change most directly attacks the latency cliff?
options: Switch the vectors to the cached tier so they are pre-loaded at startup
Use a faster SIMD instruction set
Increase the number of segments
Compress the vectors (for example to int8 or PQ codes) so the navigation data fits in RAM, and re-rank with full vectors
explain: Pre-loading cannot fit 31 GB into 16 GB, and SIMD speed is irrelevant when waiting on the SSD. Shrinking what the search touches per hop, and reading exact vectors only for the final re-rank, is exactly the DiskANN-style pattern.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
question: In the naive grouping on 8 GPUs (train 1-4-2, gen 1-2-2-2), why must G2 keep extra memory after the transition?
options: G2 is a pipeline boundary and must buffer activations
Its generation half (q3+q4) does not contain its training quarter (q2), so q2 must be kept for the next training stage
G2 hosts the controller
Consecutive grouping doubles the KV cache on even ranks
explain: Under consecutive TP grouping, G2 is rank 1 of [G1,G2] and gets q3+q4. Its training shard q2 is not inside that, so it must be stored separately until training resumes. The paper marks G2, G3, G6 and G7 as the GPUs with this redundancy.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions
question: Video-ChatGPT keeps T + N tokens by averaging over space and over time separately. Which question is it worst at?
options: What objects appear in the video?
Is the video indoors or outdoors?
Did the person pick up the cup before or after opening the door?
What is the overall topic of the video?
explain: The N spatial tokens are averaged over all frames, and the T temporal tokens are each one averaged vector per frame. Fine spatial detail tied to a specific moment is blurred, which hurts ordering questions about small actions.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Keep S = 256 tokens per frame and double the clip from 16 to 32 frames. What happens to the attention pair counts?
options: Every term doubles, so the ratio stays at 15.1
Spatial pairs double to 2,097,152, temporal pairs quadruple to 262,144, full attention quadruples to 67,108,864
Spatial pairs quadruple and temporal pairs double
Nothing changes because attention is per frame
explain: Spatial is T S squared, linear in T. Temporal is S T squared, quadratic in T but small while T is much less than S. Full is (TS) squared. The ST total is 2,359,296, so the advantage grows to TS/(S+T) = 28.4x.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
question: A team wants to train an RL agent for an Atari game cheaply using imagined experience, and they can collect actions and rewards by playing. Which approach fits best?
options: A model-based RL world model trained on their own action-labelled transitions, such as DreamerV3 or DIAMOND
A Genie-style model trained on unlabelled internet video, since labels are unnecessary
A text-to-video model prompted with the game's name
No world model: imagined experience cannot train agents
explain: When actions and rewards are available, action-conditioned world models built for RL (DreamerV3's latent imagination, DIAMOND's diffusion model with an Atari 100k mean HNS of 1.46) are the direct fit. Genie's latent actions solve a different problem: learning control from video with no labels.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: A model mixes a backend that reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Does the runner reorder?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes, with threshold 1. The runner takes the minimum and ignores None
Only on steps that contain no prefills
explain: `calculate_reorder_batch_threshold` reduces with a min that skips None. One batch order is shared by all layers, so the smallest threshold wins, and backends that need no order are unaffected.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
question: Why does a failed compare&swap make the consensus protocol work for any number of processes, while a lost test&set does not?
options: CAS is faster than test&set on modern hardware
CAS uses more memory, so it can store all inputs
test&set is not atomic
A failed CAS returns the stored value, which is the winner's input; a lost test&set returns only a bit
explain: The losers' problem is identifying the winner. CAS writes the winner's value into the shared word and hands it back to every loser. test&set returns 1 to every loser and carries no identity.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
question: A 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid covers 90N to 90S. Why does it have 721 rows instead of 720?
options: Because ERA5 adds one row of padding for convolutions
Because both poles are grid rows, so there are 720 intervals and 721 edges
Because the equator is stored twice, once per hemisphere
Because 721 is required to make the grid divisible by 4
explain: 180 degrees divided by 0.25 gives 720 intervals; counting the endpoints 90N and 90S gives 721 rows. Longitude wraps around, so 0 and 360 are the same column and there are exactly 1440.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Uncertainty: GenCast's diffusion ensembles and CRPS
question: Why does GenCast start each forecast step from fresh noise rather than from the previous step's output plus a small perturbation?
options: Diffusion models cannot accept conditioning inputs
Sampling from noise each step lets the model draw a new plausible state from the learned conditional distribution, giving sharp, distinct members
Noise makes the model run faster on TPUs
It removes the need for ERA5 initial conditions
explain: The diffusion model represents p(X(t+1) given X(t), X(t-1)). Each fresh noise draw yields a different sample of that distribution, so trajectories diverge realistically. The previous states still enter as conditioning, and forecasts still start from ERA5 plus perturbations.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
question: A Tokio worker's local queue is full (256 tasks) when it schedules one more. What happens?
options: The ring doubles to 512 slots
The new task waits until a slot frees up
128 queued tasks plus the new one, 129 in total, move to the global queue
Only the new task goes to the global queue, always
explain: Tokio never grows the ring. push_overflow claims the whole queue with one CAS, keeps the older 128 tasks locally and links the newer 128, plus the new task, into the mutex-protected global queue in one batch. (If a steal is already in progress the new task alone goes to the global queue, since the steal will free space.)

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why the loss plunges during the decay: the river valley picture
question: In the river valley picture, why is the loss during the stable stage a bad indicator of how good the model will be after cooldown?
options: Because the validation set changes between stages
Because the high LR keeps the hill component elevated, hiding river progress that the decay will reveal
Because the stable stage only learns embeddings
Because the loss is computed with dropout on during the stable stage
explain: Loss = river + hill. A high LR inflates the hill part through bouncing between steep walls, so the plateau mostly reflects noise level, not lack of progress. The decay removes the hill part and the accumulated river progress shows up.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
question: Your proxy receives bytes on one TCP socket and forwards them to another. A teammate suggests `sendfile(out_sock, in_sock, NULL, n)`. What happens?
options: It works and is zero-copy end to end
It fails, because in_fd must support mmap-like operations and a socket does not
It works but copies through user space
It fails, because out_fd may not be a socket
explain: sendfile reads from something with page-cache-like pages, a regular file. A socket is not that, so the call fails with EINVAL. Forwarding between sockets needs splice with a pipe in the middle (lesson 3). out_fd being a socket is the classic use case, so the last option is wrong.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
question: CLIP averages 80 prompt embeddings per class instead of averaging 80 sets of predicted probabilities. What does that buy at inference time?
options: Higher accuracy, because averaging probabilities is mathematically invalid
It removes the need for a temperature parameter
The ensemble costs the same as one prompt: one cached text vector per class, one image encoding per input
It lets CLIP output several labels per image
explain: Averaging in embedding space collapses the 80 prompts into one vector per class ahead of time. At inference, each image is still compared with exactly one vector per class, so the ensemble is free once the averages are cached. The paper gives exactly this reason.
